title: Permeability and saturation measured through the reservoir volume

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a way to map permeability and hydrocarbon saturation throughout a reservoir volume, with predictions that hold at wells withheld from the analysis. Permeability describes how readily rock transmits fluid; saturation describes how much of its pore space is occupied by particular fluids. The intended advance is reliable information between and beyond existing wells, with a stated spatial resolution and uncertainty. It remains a proposed capability; the supplied evidence does not establish that it has been achieved.

Conceptual scope: a porosity or acoustic-impedance image would not by itself establish this capability. The measurement must distinguish the ability to transmit fluid from the amount of pore space and must estimate hydrocarbon occupancy separately. A reservoir-volume map need not resolve every pore or provide continuous meter-scale coverage. Its defining feature is independently validated information about both properties away from the wells used to construct it.

significance.text: Conditional significance: reliable permeability and saturation maps would reduce uncertainty about reservoir properties away from existing measurement locations. Together, they could help distinguish rock containing hydrocarbons from rock through which fluids can move readily. This information could improve well placement, identify targets for further investigation and guide recovery planning before additional wells supply those measurements.

Those benefits would not make the maps self-sufficient drilling or recovery decisions. A permeability estimate does not alone establish connected flow paths across a reservoir, and hydrocarbon saturation does not establish how much oil can be recovered economically. Pressure, fluid behavior, barriers, operating constraints and economics would still matter. Improved decisions and increased recovery are downstream possibilities that would need their own demonstrations.

The historical context is a broad engineering ambition to improve subsurface imaging. According to the supplied review, D. Nathan Meehan’s JPT article, The Grand Challenges for Engineering, lists high-resolution subsurface imaging among the SPE Research and Development Committee’s challenges. The retained article displays December 31, 2015, correcting the research bibliography’s 2016 date. It does not establish a historical requirement for continuous meter-scale maps of saturation, pressure and rock properties, or demonstrate such a method. PET-08 therefore retains independent reservoir-volume permeability and saturation mapping as its core without adopting that specific resolution requirement.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability, as defined by this proposal, is a field-scale measurement and interpretation method that can distinguish permeability and hydrocarbon saturation well enough to predict both at independent locations. It must show that the observations constrain those properties, rather than merely reproducing assumptions or correlations learned from nearby wells. Whether any existing method already meets this definition remains unresolved in the supplied evidence.

The research identifies an indirect-sensitivity problem: elastic observations principally concern stiffness and impedance, while proposed permeability estimates depend on attenuation, dispersion or rock-physics relationships. It also reports that different combinations of rock and fluid properties can produce similar observations. These are relevant proposed barriers to a unique interpretation, but the cited 2025 review has no retained source text in the package. The detailed mechanisms and their applicability therefore remain unverified here.

The research also identifies weak fluid contrast, thin beds and stiff carbonate rocks as difficult settings for saturation estimation. Its earlier claim that saturation becomes invisible in these settings is too absolute: the package does not establish a general detectability boundary. The engineering question is what sensitivity and uncertainty a particular method achieves under specified rock, fluid, thickness and acquisition conditions. Likewise, a relationship between an observable and local permeability would still require separate evidence before being interpreted as a map of connected flow paths.

Engineering synthesis: the method must reconcile the different volumes sampled by remote observations and well reference measurements, quantify uncertainty, and generalize across reservoir types. It must also separate observational information from calibration assumptions and demonstrate a useful tradeoff among coverage, resolution, acquisition burden and cost. Fine measurements near a borehole would contribute evidence, but would not alone establish reliable coverage throughout a field.

current_state.text: The retained historical evidence establishes recognition of a broad subsurface-imaging challenge. The supplied review reports that the JPT article’s identity and complete extracted body were verified, with no flagged truncation. That article does not establish present-day feasibility, the performance of particular seismic or fiber methods, or the absence of a method meeting PET-08. Its historical challenge framing cannot establish that the capability remained open on November 1, 2026.

The research cites Advances in theoretical and technical approaches for seismic prediction of reservoir permeability, attributed to Lele Wei and colleagues and dated October 27, 2025. It reports limitations involving petrophysical assumptions, scale and non-uniqueness for dispersion methods; unstable inversions for pore-structure constraints; and geologically implausible extrapolation in machine-learning predictions. The research says it used only the abstract. However, neither that abstract nor the full article was retained, so the supplied review could not verify the bibliographic identity, findings or extent of access. These remain reported findings, rather than established conclusions of this record.

The research attributes to Muggeridge and colleagues’ 2014 paper, Recovery rates, enhanced oil recovery and technological limits, the observation that four-dimensional seismic can reveal bypassed oil at scales of hundreds of meters horizontally and tens of meters vertically, while much remaining oil occurs at smaller scales. These quantitative figures are preserved as an attributed report. No artifact of the paper was retained, so the supplied review could not verify the figures, their conditions or the statement about remaining oil. They should not be treated as universal resolution limits for all seismic methods.

The research describes seismic imaging of structure and favorable fluid changes, time-lapse seismic and borehole fiber monitoring during production, and finer measurements near wells from fiber or crosswell surveys. The supplied technical material is insufficient to establish their demonstrated performance or field-wide reach. Similarly, the earlier assertion that no published method constitutes a remote permeability log is not established: the package contains no bounded contemporary search record. Missing technical artifacts limit verification; they do not show that the reported results are false or that the proposed capability is impossible.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: produce reservoir-volume maps of permeability and hydrocarbon saturation in both a clastic field and a carbonate field, then test them at wells withheld from inversion, calibration and model selection. Fix predictions before revealing the validation measurements, and make the separation of training and validation information auditable.
completion_criteria.label: Clastic and carbonate property maps validate at fully withheld wells

completion_criteria.text: Before testing, specify the map’s spatial support, coverage and resolution; the independent reference measurements; acceptable errors for each property; and how uncertainty will be evaluated. Compare quantities at compatible spatial scales so that a coarse-volume prediction is not judged as though it were a point measurement. Report errors and uncertainty calibration for permeability and saturation separately, including difficult locations and failed predictions. The package supplies no justified numerical tolerances, so none are adopted here.
completion_criteria.label: Report scale-compatible permeability and saturation errors and uncertainty calibration

completion_criteria.text: Evaluate practical usefulness through a predefined drilling decision rule, while accounting separately for other geological and economic inputs. Agreement with a drill-or-don’t-drill outcome would be insufficient by itself: an inaccurate property map can coincide with the right decision for unrelated reasons. Convincing evidence would combine accurate property estimates with demonstrated decision value.
completion_criteria.label: Accurate property estimates demonstrate value under predefined drilling decisions

completion_criteria.text: For this proposal, a porosity volume alone, a permeability field fitted to production history, or a dense fiber array confined to one well would not satisfy the intended independent reservoir-volume measurement requirement. These can be useful complementary methods; the exclusions define what PET-08 is trying to demonstrate. Fine-scale near-well results must be accompanied by validation of the claimed coverage away from those wells.
completion_criteria.label: Validate independent reservoir-volume measurements across claimed coverage beyond wells

completion_criteria.text: Reproducibility should include sufficient acquisition, processing, calibration and validation detail for an independent team to repeat the assessment, with practical limits on acquisition time, cost and deployment stated explicitly. Successful tests in two reservoir classes would establish demonstrated breadth under the tested conditions. They would not establish literal universality across geology, fluids, depths or operating conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Independent assessment is reproducible with practical limits explicitly stated

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison based on the supplied titles and research: PET-01, Blind prediction of multiphase reservoir flow, concerns predicting how fluids evolve and move. PET-08 concerns measuring reservoir properties that could constrain such predictions. PET-02, Conventional-oil recovery at gas-field recovery factors, concerns a recovery outcome; improved characterization could help pursue it, but a map does not supply a displacement mechanism or establish the resulting recovery factor. Neither entry’s detailed specification was supplied.

Title-based comparison: PET-05, Shale-oil recovery from the matrix, and PET-09, Bitumen that flows at native reservoir temperature, concern accessing or mobilizing hydrocarbons. PET-08 could provide relevant characterization, but it does not itself release oil from a matrix or make bitumen flow. PET-03, Commercial gas production from methane hydrate, concerns producing a different resource; applicability of PET-08 to hydrate-bearing formations would require its own evidence.

Title-based comparison: PET-04, Industrial in-situ conversion of oil-shale kerogen; PET-06, Hydrogen from petroleum reservoirs, with the other products left underground; and PET-11, In-reservoir conversion of bitumen to pipeline-specification crude, concern subsurface conversion processes. Property measurements might support characterization or monitoring, but PET-08 does not demonstrate conversion chemistry, product quality, containment or commercial performance.

Title-based comparison: PET-07, Deep well construction without a steep depth penalty, concerns constructing access to the subsurface. PET-08 concerns information across the reservoir, including away from well access. PET-10, A pressure plan with a prospectively tested earthquake bound, concerns operational pressure management and a tested seismicity constraint. Permeability information could inform such planning, but permeability and saturation maps alone do not establish pressure evolution or an earthquake bound. These relationships preserve the entries as distinct innovations.

unresolved_issues: The 2025 permeability review and 2014 recovery paper have no retained artifacts. Their identities, detailed conclusions, quantitative context and the claimed abstract-only access remain unverified.
The package contains no bounded contemporary search record establishing whether a method meeting PET-08 existed as of November 1, 2026.
Spatial support, reference measurements, numerical error tolerances, uncertainty requirements and acceptable acquisition costs remain to be defined.
The relationship between any proposed observable, estimated permeability and reservoir-scale connected flow paths requires separate validation.
Detailed specifications for the related concepts were not supplied; comparisons beyond PET-08’s research are necessarily limited to their titles.

The review’s recommendation to replace unverified technical detail with a general evidence-gap statement was not adopted wholesale. Useful research detail was retained as explicitly attributed or conditional material, preserving explanatory substance without treating it as verified.

brief.title: Maps of oil, gas and how easily rock carries fluids
possible: Before drilling another well, reservoir teams could map how readily rock lets fluids pass and how much of its pore space holds oil or gas. Those properties are called permeability and hydrocarbon saturation. The maps would extend between and beyond existing wells, with stated detail and uncertainty.
why: Knowing where oil and gas sit, alongside how easily fluids can move through the rock, could help teams choose well locations, identify targets for investigation and plan recovery.

sources.showed: This paper examines recovery rates, methods for extracting additional oil and technological limits.
sources.cited_for: It supports the discussion of imaging oil left behind during production.
sources.not_established: It does not establish independently validated maps of both properties throughout a reservoir.

sources.showed: This review examines theoretical and technical approaches to predicting reservoir permeability from seismic observations, which use sound waves.
sources.cited_for: It supports the discussion of difficulties in estimating permeability indirectly.
sources.not_established: It does not establish reliable maps of permeability and saturation away from the wells used to build them.

sources.showed: Meehan described the Society of Petroleum Engineers committee’s recognition of detailed underground imaging as an engineering challenge.
sources.cited_for: It establishes the broader ambition to improve underground imaging.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate a method for mapping permeability and saturation.

shown: Muggeridge and colleagues describe seismic imaging repeated over time revealing oil bypassed during production. That is a step toward locating remaining oil, but independently validated maps of both permeability and saturation throughout a reservoir remain a proposed capability.
missing: Maps must predict both properties at wells excluded from every stage of building and choosing the model.
Measurements must distinguish the properties themselves from assumptions and correlations borrowed from nearby wells.
Validation must cover the claimed volume away from wells, with useful detail, uncertainty and practical acquisition costs.

milestones.label: Maps succeed at fully withheld wells across rock types
milestones.explanation: Maps would have to predict both properties in clastic and carbonate reservoirs, the required rock types, at wells excluded from all model development. This would test whether predictions hold beyond familiar wells.

milestones.label: Errors and uncertainty hold at the stated map scale
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to set coverage, detail and acceptable errors beforehand, compare matching volumes and assess uncertainty separately for each property. This would establish what the maps reliably resolve.

milestones.label: Accurate maps improve predefined drilling decisions
milestones.explanation: A predefined drilling rule would have to demonstrate value alongside accurate property estimates, accounting separately for other inputs. This would link measurement quality to practical usefulness.

milestones.label: Independent measurements validate coverage beyond wells
milestones.explanation: Independent tests would have to validate both properties throughout the claimed coverage away from wells. This would establish that local measurements or fitted models provide reliable information across the reservoir.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results within stated practical limits
milestones.explanation: An independent team would have to repeat the assessment with acquisition time, cost and deployment limits stated. This would establish reproducibility and the conditions under which the method works.

uncertain: Whether an existing method already meets the full definition remains unresolved.
Acceptable errors, map detail, uncertainty and acquisition costs still need to be defined.
Permeability estimates alone do not establish connected flow paths, and oil or gas occupancy alone does not establish economical recovery.

page.title: Reservoir-volume permeability and hydrocarbon-saturation mapping
page.definition: Three-dimensional maps separately estimate permeability, the ability of rock to transmit fluid, and hydrocarbon saturation, the fraction of pore space occupied by oil or gas. Estimates between and beyond calibration wells are validated at withheld wells, at a stated spatial resolution and uncertainty.

goal.need: Muggeridge and colleagues reported recovery factors of 20–40% for mature oilfields and described repeated seismic surveys identifying bypassed oil over hundreds of metres horizontally and tens of metres vertically. Permeability heterogeneity affects how much reservoir volume injected fluids sweep. DOE identified the gap between centimetre-scale borehole information and regional seismic imaging as a reservoir-characterization challenge.

figures.caption: Recovery and imaging scales reported in a 2014 review.
figures.note: The imaging scales describe the applications discussed in the review; they are not universal resolution limits.

statements.body: The Society of Petroleum Engineers R&D Committee identified subsurface imaging as a grand challenge, as reported by SPE president D. Nathan Meehan.
statements.context: An item in the committee’s list of engineering grand challenges.

statements.body: The US Department of Energy’s SubTER Grand Challenge Roundtable identified reservoir composition, permeability and fluids as a characterization challenge.
statements.quote: The task of describing mineralogical/organic matter compositions, permeability, porosity, and saturating fluids within a subsurface reservoir remains a first-order technical challenge.

statements.body: The US Department of Energy’s National Energy Technology Laboratory funded seismic estimation of reservoir fluid properties through project DE-FC26-04NT15503.
statements.quote: The project goal is to develop seismic-based technology that quantifies a reservoir’s fluid-saturation and fluid-mobility properties.
statements.context: Fluid mobility depends on permeability and fluid viscosity. The project ran from 1 January 2005 to 31 May 2007.

completion.title: Both reservoir-volume maps pass a prospective field test at withheld wells.
completion.criterion: A field survey yields separate three-dimensional permeability and hydrocarbon-saturation maps between and beyond calibration wells. Both meet application-specific error, spatial-resolution and coverage limits published before testing, using scale-matched references at wells excluded from calibration and model selection. Adding the survey observations must reduce prediction error for each property relative to the same workflow without those observations. Numerical acceptance limits remain unspecified because no outside body’s joint threshold was located.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no joint acceptance threshold was located in the searched society, government, roadmap and validation literature.
completion.basis: SPE grand-challenge material, DOE SubTER and NETL imaging programmes, NPC formation-evaluation needs, and literature on seismic inversion and blind-well validation were searched for a joint acceptance test. No published numerical completion threshold was located. This provisional test combines the stated imaging goal with independent prediction tests. The opened results do not establish completion.

milestones.title: A laboratory method separately recovers permeability and hydrocarbon saturation.
milestones.criterion: At controlled pressure and temperature, vary permeability and hydrocarbon saturation independently and recover each against flow and fluid-volume measurements, within acceptance limits published before testing. Partial evidence: Adam and colleagues tested five carbonate samples with 20–30% porosity and 0.03–58.1 mD permeability; attenuation increased by 250% on average when brine replaced liquid butane. This establishes fluid sensitivity, rather than separate recovery of both properties.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; no published laboratory acceptance threshold for separate recovery of both properties was located. The cited experiment establishes a precursor result.

milestones.title: Field methods pass separate blind-well tests of permeability and hydrocarbon saturation.
milestones.criterion: For each property separately, field observations predict scale-matched reference measurements at wells excluded from calibration and model selection, within acceptance limits published before testing. Wei and colleagues specify blind-well validation for permeability without a numerical pass limit. Guo and colleagues used two wells, withholding one, and reported a water-saturation correlation of 0.693; they also assigned a prior mean of 0.68 while reporting test-well water saturation of 0.6–0.7. The latter does not establish complete information withholding.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; blind-well comparison is a published validation practice, but no common numerical acceptance threshold for both properties was located.

milestones.title: One field survey produces both property maps over the same three-dimensional reservoir volume.
milestones.criterion: An integrated field system produces separate permeability and hydrocarbon-saturation maps over the same stated three-dimensional volume and meets prospectively published calibration-site error and resolution limits. Blind-well acceptance remains the completion test. Partial evidence: Penna and Lupinacci generated permeability volumes for one carbonate reservoir, Mero. Côrte and colleagues estimated saturation changes in one field, Schiehallion, but lacked repeated saturation logs for direct validation. These separate studies do not establish the integrated result.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; no published acceptance threshold for an integrated field prototype preceding joint blind-well validation was located.

not_found: No common numerical acceptance threshold for joint reservoir-volume permeability and hydrocarbon-saturation mapping was found in the searched SPE, DOE/NETL and NPC documents.
No outside body’s pass limits were located for the three milestones; their Atlas tests remain provisional until application-specific limits are published.
No opened study established completion of the joint reservoir-volume blind-well test.
The full Mero paper PDF exceeded the retrieval limit; its opened publisher abstract supports the stated three-dimensional mapping result.
